## 1. Core Learning Objectives & Mathematical Competencies

By completing this laboratory, students master four interconnected pillars of electrical and dynamical systems engineering:

:::: {.pillar-grid}

::: {.pillar-card style="border-top: 4px solid #4338ca;"}
[Pillar 1 • Time-Domain Calculus]{.pillar-tag style="color: #4338ca;"}

[Derivatives & Integrals in Circuits]{.pillar-title}

Apply $i_C(t) = C\dfrac{dv_C}{dt}$ and $v_L(t) = L\dfrac{di_L}{dt}$ to prove why differentiating a sine wave ($\dfrac{d}{dt}[\sin(\omega t)] = \omega\cos(\omega t)$) produces an exact $+90^\circ$ phase advance and scales peak amplitude by $\omega$.
:::

::: {.pillar-card style="border-top: 4px solid #0284c7;"}
[Pillar 2 • Numerical Computation]{.pillar-tag style="color: #0284c7;"}

[MATLAB Discrete Differentiation]{.pillar-title}

Build `.m` scripts from scratch using discrete time vectors, finite-difference numerical derivatives (`diff(v_s) ./ diff(t)`), and dual-axis oscilloscope waveform plots (`yyaxis left` and `yyaxis right`).
:::

::: {.pillar-card style="border-top: 4px solid #059669;"}
[Pillar 3 • Frequency-Domain Vectors]{.pillar-tag style="color: #059669;"}

[Phasor Algebra & KVL Geometry]{.pillar-title}

Transform differential operators into complex algebra ($\dfrac{d}{dt} \leftrightarrow j\omega$ and $\int dt \leftrightarrow \dfrac{1}{j\omega}$) and verify Kirchhoff's Voltage Law via polar (`compass`) and tip-to-tail (`quiver`) vector plots.
:::

::: {.pillar-card style="border-top: 4px solid #d97706;"}
[Pillar 4 • Dynamical Systems]{.pillar-tag style="color: #d97706;"}

[Simulink Continuous Integrators]{.pillar-title}

Translate 1st- and 2nd-order differential equations into continuous-time Simulink integrator feedback loops ($\dfrac{1}{s}$) to observe exponential charging and underdamped RLC ringing.
:::

::::

## 3. Part I: The Calculus of Sine Waves & Time-Domain Derivatives in MATLAB

### Why Differentiating a Sine Wave Produces a $+90^\circ$ Phase Shift
In an ideal resistor, voltage and current are proportional ($v_R = i_R R$), so their waveforms peak and cross zero at the exact same instant. In reactive components, however, voltage and current are linked by **calculus**:

$$\text{Capacitor: } i_C(t) = C \frac{dv_C(t)}{dt} \qquad \Bigg| \qquad \text{Inductor: } v_L(t) = L \frac{di_L(t)}{dt}$$

When we drive a capacitor with a sinusoidal voltage $v_C(t) = V_m \sin(\omega t)$, the chain rule of calculus gives:

$$i_C(t) = C \frac{d}{dt}\Big[V_m \sin(\omega t)\Big] = \underbrace{\omega C V_m}_{I_m} \cos(\omega t) = I_m \sin(\omega t + 90^\circ)$$

```{=html}
<!-- Visual Diagram of Derivative Slope vs Phase Shift -->
```

### How MATLAB Computes a Numerical Derivative (`diff`)
In digital oscilloscopes and MATLAB scripts, continuous waveforms are stored as discrete vectors sampled every $\Delta t$ seconds. MATLAB's `diff(v_s)` command subtracts each voltage sample from the next ($v_{k+1} - v_k$). Dividing element-by-element (`./`) by `diff(t)` computes the instantaneous rise-over-run derivative slope at every microsecond:

$$\frac{dv}{dt} \approx \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v(t_{k+1}) - v(t_k)}{t_{k+1} - t_k}$$

```matlab
% =========================================================================
% PART 1A: NUMERICAL TIME DERIVATIVE OF A CAPACITOR IN MATLAB
% =========================================================================
clc; clear; close all;

% 1. Create a time vector from 0 to 0.05 s (3 cycles of 60 Hz) in 10 us steps
t = 0 : 1e-5 : 0.05;

% 2. Define the 60 Hz sinusoidal voltage: v_s(t) = 12*sin(2*pi*60*t)
f = 60;                         % Frequency = 60 Hz
w = 2 * pi * f;                 % Angular frequency = 376.99 rad/s
v_s = 12 * sin(w * t);          % Applied capacitor voltage [Volts]

% 3. Compute the numerical time derivative dv_s / dt
dv_dt = diff(v_s) ./ diff(t);   % Rise-over-run slope [Volts/sec]
t_diff = t(1:end-1);            % Trim last time point to match diff() length

% 4. Apply Capacitor Calculus Law: i_C(t) = C * (dv_s / dt)
C = 10e-6;                      % Capacitance = 10 uF
i_C = C * dv_dt;                % Resulting capacitor current [Amps]

% 5. Dual-Axis Oscilloscope Plot
figure(1);
yyaxis left;
plot(t, v_s, 'b-', 'LineWidth', 2);
ylabel('Capacitor Voltage v_C(t) [Volts]'); ylim([-15, 15]);

yyaxis right;
plot(t_diff, i_C, 'r--', 'LineWidth', 2);
ylabel('Capacitor Current i_C(t) [Amps]'); ylim([-0.06, 0.06]);
xlabel('Time t [seconds]');
title('Ideal Capacitor: Current Leads Voltage by 90^\circ (i_C = C dv_C/dt)');
grid on;
```

## 4. Part II: Interactive Phasor Bench (`compass` Polar & `quiver` Tip-to-Tail KVL)

By Euler's formula ($e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta$), differentiating a sinusoid in the time domain is equivalent to multiplying its complex phasor by $j\omega$ in the frequency domain, while integrating is equivalent to dividing by $j\omega$:

$$\frac{d}{dt} \iff j\omega = \omega\angle +90^\circ \qquad \Bigg| \qquad \int dt \iff \frac{1}{j\omega} = -j\frac{1}{\omega} = \frac{1}{\omega}\angle -90^\circ$$

### Interactive Phasor & Time-Domain Explorer

```{=html}
<script>
let pMode = 'RL';
function setPhasorMode(m) {
  pMode = m;
  document.getElementById('btnRL').style.background = m === 'RL' ? '#1e1b4b' : '#e2e8f0';
  document.getElementById('btnRL').style.color = m === 'RL' ? '#fff' : '#1e293b';
  document.getElementById('btnRC').style.background = m === 'RC' ? '#1e1b4b' : '#e2e8f0';
  document.getElementById('btnRC').style.color = m === 'RC' ? '#fff' : '#1e293b';
  document.getElementById('btnRLC').style.background = m === 'RLC' ? '#1e1b4b' : '#e2e8f0';
  document.getElementById('btnRLC').style.color = m === 'RLC' ? '#fff' : '#1e293b';

  if (m === 'RL') {
    document.getElementById('slVs').value = 20;
    document.getElementById('slR').value = 30;
    document.getElementById('slX').value = 38;
    document.getElementById('lblXTitle').textContent = 'Inductive Reactance X_L:';
  } else if (m === 'RC') {
    document.getElementById('slVs').value = 24;
    document.getElementById('slR').value = 40;
    document.getElementById('slX').value = 53;
    document.getElementById('lblXTitle').textContent = 'Capacitive Reactance X_C:';
  } else {
    document.getElementById('slVs').value = 24;
    document.getElementById('slR').value = 25;
    document.getElementById('slX').value = 20;
    document.getElementById('lblXTitle').textContent = 'Net Reactance (X_L - X_C):';
  }
  updatePhasorWidget();
}

function drawArrow(ctx, x1, y1, x2, y2, color, label, dashed=false) {
  const headlen = 9;
  const dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
  const angle = Math.atan2(dy, dx);
  ctx.save();
  ctx.strokeStyle = color;
  ctx.fillStyle = color;
  ctx.lineWidth = 2.4;
  if (dashed) ctx.setLineDash([5, 4]);
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(x1, y1);
  ctx.lineTo(x2, y2);
  ctx.stroke();
  ctx.setLineDash([]);
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(x2, y2);
  ctx.lineTo(x2 - headlen * Math.cos(angle - Math.PI / 6), y2 - headlen * Math.sin(angle - Math.PI / 6));
  ctx.lineTo(x2 - headlen * Math.cos(angle + Math.PI / 6), y2 - headlen * Math.sin(angle + Math.PI / 6));
  ctx.closePath();
  ctx.fill();
  if (label) {
    ctx.font = 'bold 12px "Computer Modern Serif", Georgia, serif';
    ctx.fillText(label, x2 + (dx >= 0 ? 6 : -38), y2 + (dy >= 0 ? 12 : -6));
  }
  ctx.restore();
}

function updatePhasorWidget() {
  const Vs = parseFloat(document.getElementById('slVs').value);
  const R = parseFloat(document.getElementById('slR').value);
  const Xmag = parseFloat(document.getElementById('slX').value);
  const X = pMode === 'RC' ? -Xmag : Xmag;

  document.getElementById('lblVs').textContent = Vs + ' V';
  document.getElementById('lblR').textContent = R + ' Ω';
  document.getElementById('lblX').textContent = (X >= 0 ? '+' : '') + X + ' Ω';

  const Zmag = Math.hypot(R, X);
  const Zang = Math.atan2(X, R);
  const Imag = Vs / Zmag;
  const Iang = -Zang;

  const VR_re = Imag * R * Math.cos(Iang);
  const VR_im = Imag * R * Math.sin(Iang);
  const VX_re = -Imag * X * Math.sin(Iang);
  const VX_im = Imag * X * Math.cos(Iang);

  const VRmag = Math.hypot(VR_re, VR_im);
  const VXmag = Math.hypot(VX_re, VX_im);
  const deg = r => (r * 180 / Math.PI).toFixed(1);

  const c1 = document.getElementById('cvCompass');
  const ctx1 = c1.getContext('2d');
  ctx1.clearRect(0, 0, c1.width, c1.height);
  const cx = 155, cy = 130, scale = 3.4;

  ctx1.strokeStyle = '#e2e8f0';
  ctx1.lineWidth = 1;
  [35, 70, 102].forEach(r => {
    ctx1.beginPath(); ctx1.arc(cx, cy, r, 0, 2*Math.PI); ctx1.stroke();
  });
  ctx1.strokeStyle = '#94a3b8';
  ctx1.beginPath(); ctx1.moveTo(15, cy); ctx1.lineTo(295, cy);
  ctx1.moveTo(cx, 15); ctx1.lineTo(cx, 245); ctx1.stroke();

  drawArrow(ctx1, cx, cy, cx + Vs*scale, cy, '#0f172a', 'Vs');
  drawArrow(ctx1, cx, cy, cx + VR_re*scale, cy - VR_im*scale, '#2563eb', 'V_R');
  drawArrow(ctx1, cx, cy, cx + VX_re*scale, cy - VX_im*scale, '#dc2626', pMode === 'RC' ? 'V_C' : 'V_L');
  drawArrow(ctx1, cx, cy, cx + (VR_re*0.65)*scale, cy - (VR_im*0.65)*scale, '#059669', 'I', true);

  const c2 = document.getElementById('cvQuiver');
  const ctx2 = c2.getContext('2d');
  ctx2.clearRect(0, 0, c2.width, c2.height);
  const qx = 45, qy = 130, qscale = 7.2;

  ctx2.strokeStyle = '#cbd5e1';
  ctx2.beginPath(); ctx2.moveTo(15, qy); ctx2.lineTo(295, qy);
  ctx2.moveTo(qx, 20); ctx2.lineTo(qx, 240); ctx2.stroke();

  const tipVRx = qx + VR_re * qscale;
  const tipVRy = qy - VR_im * qscale;
  const tipVsx = qx + Vs * qscale;

  drawArrow(ctx2, qx, qy, tipVRx, tipVRy, '#2563eb', '1. V_R');
  drawArrow(ctx2, tipVRx, tipVRy, tipVsx, qy, '#dc2626', pMode === 'RC' ? '2. V_C' : '2. V_L');
  drawArrow(ctx2, qx, qy, tipVsx, qy, '#0f172a', '3. V_s', true);

  document.getElementById('phasorReadout').innerHTML = `
    <div><span style="color:#94a3b8;">Impedance Z:</span> <strong>${Zmag.toFixed(2)}∠${deg(Zang)}° Ω</strong></div>
    <div><span style="color:#6ee7b7;">Current I:</span> <strong>${Imag.toFixed(3)}∠${deg(Iang)}° A</strong></div>
    <div><span style="color:#93c5fd;">Resistor V_R:</span> <strong>${VRmag.toFixed(2)}∠${deg(Iang)}° V</strong></div>
    <div><span style="color:#fca5a5;">Reactive ${pMode==='RC'?'V_C':'V_L'}:</span> <strong>${VXmag.toFixed(2)}∠${deg(Iang + (X>=0?Math.PI/2:-Math.PI/2))}° V</strong></div>
  `;
}
document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', updatePhasorWidget);
</script>
```

## 5. Part III: What is Simulink & How Does It Model Circuits Visually?

### Why Engineers Use Simulink Alongside MATLAB
While **MATLAB** executes sequential lines of text code, **Simulink** is a graphical block-diagram environment designed for modeling dynamical systems governed by differential equations. Instead of solving differential equations by hand before coding, Simulink allows students to wire mathematical operations (**Sum**, **Gain**, and **Integrator `1/s`** blocks) directly into a closed-loop feedback system:

1. **The Integrator Block ($\frac{1}{s}$) as a Calculus Engine:** In Laplace notation, multiplying by $\frac{1}{s}$ represents time integration ($\int dt$). If the wire entering an Integrator block carries the derivative $\frac{dv_C}{dt}$, the wire exiting that block carries the integrated state variable $v_C(t)$ itself.
2. **Isolate the Highest Derivative:** For a 1st-order Series RC circuit ($V_s = RC\frac{dv_C}{dt} + v_C$), isolating the derivative yields:
   $$\frac{dv_C}{dt} = \frac{1}{RC}\Big[V_s(t) - v_C(t)\Big]$$

## 6. Complete Lab Walkthrough & Student Exercises

::: {.panel-tabset}

## 🧭 Module 0: MATLAB Primer

### Absolute Beginner's Guide to MATLAB & `.m` Files
While single calculations in the **Command Window** disappear when MATLAB closes, sequences of commands saved in an **`.m` Script File** create reproducible engineering simulations.

1. **Create Your Script:** Click **New Script** on the **HOME** ribbon and save as `Circuit_Lab_LastName.m` (use only letters, numbers, and underscores).
2. **Four Essential MATLAB Symbols:**
   * **`%` (Comment):** Ignored by MATLAB; used to document engineering units.
   * **`;` (Semicolon):** Suppresses screen printing of 5,000-element arrays.
   * **`:` (Colon Operator):** Generates evenly spaced time arrays (`t = 0 : 1e-5 : 0.05;`).
   * **`1j` (Imaginary Unit):** Represents $\sqrt{-1} = 1\angle +90^\circ$ for complex impedance calculations.

## ⏱️ Part I: Inductor Calculus Challenge

### Student Exercise (Task 1B): Inductor Derivative ($v_L = L\frac{di_L}{dt}$)
Below your Part 1A capacitor code, simulate an **ideal inductor** of inductance $L = 50\text{ mH}$ (`50e-3` H) driven by a sinusoidal current source $i_s(t) = 2\sin(120\pi t)\text{ A}$ by filling in the missing blanks (`___`):

```matlab
% --- PART 1B: STUDENT EXERCISE - IDEAL INDUCTOR (L = 50 mH) ---
i_s = 2 * sin(w * t);                   % 1. Inductor current: 2*sin(120*pi*t) Amps
di_dt = diff(___) ./ diff(t);           % 2. Numerical derivative di_s / dt
L = ___;                                % 3. Inductance = 50 mH (50e-3)
v_L = L * ___;                          % 4. Inductor Calculus Law: v_L = L*(di_s/dt)

figure(2);
yyaxis left;  plot(t, i_s, 'b-', 'LineWidth', 2); ylabel('Current i_L(t) [Amps]');
yyaxis right; plot(t_diff, ___, 'r--', 'LineWidth', 2); ylabel('Voltage v_L(t) [Volts]');
xlabel('Time t [seconds]'); title('Part 1B: Ideal Inductor (v_L = L di_L/dt)'); grid on;
```

## 📐 Part II: Phasor MATLAB Code

### Series RL Phasor Script (`compass` & `quiver`)
```matlab
% --- PART 2A: SERIES RL PHASOR PLOTS (compass & quiver) ---
Vs = 20 * exp(1j * 0);          % Reference source: 20 angle 0 deg V
f = 60; w = 2 * pi * f;
R = 30; L = 0.100;              % R = 30 Ohms, L = 100 mH

ZR = R;
ZL = 1j * w * L;                % Inductor impedance (+j37.70 Ohms)
Zeq = ZR + ZL;
I_phasor = Vs / Zeq;
VR = I_phasor * ZR;
VL = I_phasor * ZL;

% Polar Plot (compass) & Tip-to-Tail KVL Vector Plot (quiver)
figure(3); compass([Vs, VR, VL, 20*I_phasor]);
figure(4); hold on; grid on; axis equal;
quiver(0, 0, real(VR), imag(VR), 0, 'b', 'LineWidth', 2);
quiver(real(VR), imag(VR), real(VL), imag(VL), 0, 'r', 'LineWidth', 2);
quiver(0, 0, real(Vs), imag(Vs), 0, 'k--', 'LineWidth', 2.5);
```

## 🔄 Part III: 2nd-Order RLC Damping

### Comparing Underdamped, Critically Damped, and Overdamped Regimes
Using **Simulink Schematic 2** above ($L = 1\text{ H}$, $C = 0.2\text{ F}$, $V_s = 10\text{ V}$ step), students run three simulations across `R = 1`, `R = 4.47`, and `R = 10` $\Omega$ and verify the characteristic roots $s_{1,2} = -\alpha \pm \sqrt{\alpha^2 - \omega_0^2}$:

| Run & Resistance $R$ | Neper Freq. $\alpha = \frac{R}{2L}$ | Resonant Freq. $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$ | Characteristic Roots $s_{1,2}$ | Dynamical Regime |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Run 1: $R = 1\ \Omega$** | $0.50\text{ Np/s}$ | $2.236\text{ rad/s}$ | $-0.50 \pm j2.18\text{ s}^{-1}$ | **Underdamped Ringing** |
| **Run 2: $R = 4.47\ \Omega$** | $2.236\text{ Np/s}$ | $2.236\text{ rad/s}$ | $-2.236, -2.236\text{ s}^{-1}$ | **Critically Damped** |
| **Run 3: $R = 10\ \Omega$** | $5.00\text{ Np/s}$ | $2.236\text{ rad/s}$ | $-0.53, -9.47\text{ s}^{-1}$ | **Overdamped** |
